mcqs.question: What is the main downside of polling as an I/O strategy?
options: The CPU busy-waits in a loop checking device status, wasting cycles it could spend on other work while the device isn't ready
It cannot detect when a device is ready at all
It requires specialized hardware that most devices don't support
It only works for network devices, not storage devices
mcqs.explanation: Polling's core cost is wasted CPU cycles spent busy-waiting. It does detect readiness (in fact instantly upon check), requires no special hardware, and applies broadly across device types.

mcqs.question: What problem does DMA solve that interrupt-driven I/O alone does not?
options: DMA eliminates the need for interrupts entirely in all systems
DMA removes the CPU from the per-byte data path during bulk transfers, so CPU involvement doesn't scale with transfer size the way it would if the CPU moved every byte itself
DMA makes devices signal readiness faster than interrupts can
DMA is only relevant for read operations, not writes
mcqs.explanation: DMA specifically addresses per-byte CPU involvement in large transfers, which plain interrupt-driven I/O (without DMA) still requires. DMA still typically uses an interrupt to signal completion, doesn't change signal speed, and applies to both reads and writes.

mcqs.question: In a DMA transfer, what does the CPU actually do while the bulk data movement is happening?
options: It continuously polls the DMA controller for progress updates
It copies each byte from the DMA controller's buffer to memory itself
It is free to do other work — the DMA controller performs the transfer independently and only interrupts the CPU when the whole transfer completes
It must remain idle and cannot execute any other instructions until the transfer finishes
mcqs.explanation: The whole point of DMA is that the CPU is uninvolved during the actual transfer and only reappears at completion via an interrupt. It doesn't poll for progress, doesn't move bytes itself, and is not forced to idle.

mcqs.question: How do modern systems typically combine polling, interrupts, and DMA?
options: They pick exactly one mechanism and use it exclusively for all I/O
Polling and DMA are mutually exclusive and can never be used in the same system
DMA is used to detect readiness while interrupts move the data
Interrupts (or occasionally polling) signal that a device is ready or a request should begin, while DMA handles the actual bulk data movement once a transfer is underway
mcqs.explanation: Real systems typically layer signaling (interrupts, sometimes polling) with DMA for bulk movement, rather than using one mechanism exclusively. DMA doesn't detect readiness, and polling/DMA can coexist in the same system for different purposes.

mcqs.question: Why might a high-performance network driver switch to polling under very high packet rates instead of relying solely on interrupts?
options: Each interrupt carries fixed handling overhead, and at very high event frequency, paying that cost on every single event can exceed the cost of simply polling
Interrupts stop working entirely above a certain event frequency
Polling uses less total CPU time than interrupts under all conditions
Network cards are physically incapable of generating interrupts
mcqs.explanation: The fixed per-interrupt overhead becomes the dominant cost at very high event rates, which is why polling (or a hybrid approach) can win in that specific regime. Interrupts don't stop functioning, polling isn't universally cheaper, and network cards can generate interrupts fine.

mcqs.question: A device fires events every 1000ns; each interrupt costs 500ns of fixed overhead. What does this imply, and what do high-throughput drivers typically do about it?
options: Interrupt overhead consumes about half of available CPU time at this rate, so drivers switch to polling or coalesce interrupts under load (like Linux NAPI)
Nothing changes; interrupts always cost the same fraction of CPU time regardless of event frequency
The fixed overhead disappears entirely once the event rate exceeds 1 MHz
Polling always performs worse than interrupts, so drivers add more interrupt handlers instead
mcqs.explanation: 500ns of fixed overhead against a 1000ns inter-event gap means roughly half of CPU time goes to interrupt handling alone. Because this cost is fixed per event, it stops being amortized at high rates -- exactly why real drivers switch to polling or coalesce interrupts under bursty load (NAPI: one interrupt, then poll until the burst drains) rather than taking a full interrupt per packet.
